notes.meaning: The Lord gave these commands while Israel was still living in Egypt, before the final plague fell. He spoke directly to both Moses and Aaron, showing that both brothers were called to lead the nation in this sacred event. This law was established before the covenant at Mount Sinai, setting Israel apart as God's own people.

God reset the calendar for His people so their religious year would start in the spring, during the month of Abib (later called Nisan). Their rescue from slavery was so important that it marked the beginning of a whole new life for the nation. From then on, their year revolved around God's mighty act of saving them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that this command did not replace the older autumn civil calendar used for farming, but established a sacred calendar so the spring festival of freedom would always stand first in their count of months.

notes.meaning: Four days before the celebration, each family had to pick out a young lamb or goat and bring it into the home. Keeping the animal close for a few days gave the family time to inspect it carefully and make sure it had no flaws. It also allowed the animal to become special to the household before the sacrifice.

If a family was too small to eat an entire animal, they were told to invite their nearest neighbors to share it. God wanted the entire sacrifice to be consumed rather than wasted. The group was arranged beforehand based on how much food each person needed.

The chosen animal had to be a healthy, one-year-old male from either the sheep or the goats, completely free from disease or defect. Offering the very best animal showed deep reverence for God. Christian readers have long seen this spotless lamb as a picture of Jesus Christ, who lived a sinless life and gave Himself for others.

The families cared for the animal until the fourteenth day of the month, when the entire community slaughtered their lambs at twilight. Killing the animals in the late afternoon brought the whole nation together in one shared moment of obedience. This timing also pointed forward to the afternoon hour when Christ died on the cross.

The people collected the blood of the sacrifice and brushed it on the top and sides of the doorframe of their homes. This visible mark showed that the home was dedicated to God and under His shelter. The blood was never placed on the threshold, so no one would disrespectfully walk on it.

That night, the family gathered to eat the roasted meat along with bitter herbs and flat bread made without yeast. The bitter herbs reminded them of the hard years of cruel slavery in Egypt. The unleavened bread served as a reminder of how quickly they had to pack up and leave.

God commanded that the meat be roasted whole over the fire rather than boiled in pots or eaten raw. Roasting was the fastest way to cook the meal for people about to travel, and keeping the animal whole preserved the dignity of the sacred offering. It also set Israel's worship apart from the pagan customs of surrounding nations.

The family was not allowed to leave any leftovers for the following day. Any parts of the meat that were not eaten had to be burned with fire before sunrise. This rule kept the holy sacrifice from spoiling in the heat or being treated like common everyday food.

The people had to eat the meal dressed for travel, with their robes tucked into their belts, sandals on their feet, and walking staffs in hand. They ate quickly, ready to move the second God called them to leave. This meal was named the Passover because the Lord was about to pass over and rescue them.

The Lord announced that He would go through Egypt that night to strike down every firstborn son and firstborn beast. This terrible judgment fell upon the false gods of Egypt as well, exposing them as powerless to protect their worshippers. God proved once and for all that He alone is the true Lord of heaven and earth.

The blood on the doorposts served as a sign identifying the homes of God's people. When the Lord saw the blood, He passed over that house and spared everyone inside from the deadly plague. Safety did not depend on how good the people were, but on God's mercy and the blood of the sacrifice that covered them.

God directed Israel to celebrate this day every year as a lasting memorial for all future generations. It was designed as an ongoing festival of joy and thanksgiving for God's great redemption. Celebrating it year after year kept the memory of God's saving power fresh in every heart.

For seven full days following the Passover, the people were required to eat only bread made without yeast. Before the festival began, every family had to search their home and clear out all leaven. In Scripture, yeast often represents the quiet spread of sin, so clearing it out called God's people to live holy and obedient lives.

The first day and the seventh day of the festival were set apart for special religious gatherings, called holy assemblies. On both of these days, ordinary daily work had to stop, just like on a Sabbath. The only work allowed was preparing the food needed for each family's meals.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread was commanded because it marked the very day God led the tribes of Israel out of slavery like an army. Remembering this historical event was meant to remind them that their freedom was entirely God's doing. It became a permanent law so they would never forget who they were.

The exact time for eating unleavened bread began on the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month and ended on the evening of the twenty-first day. The biblical day began at sunset, linking the Passover supper directly to the week of unleavened bread that followed. This set a strict, seven-day boundary for the sacred feast.

No yeast of any kind was allowed in any house for the entire week of the festival. Anyone who deliberately broke this rule was cut off, meaning separated from the worshipping community. This law applied equally to native Israelites and to foreigners who had joined the faith of Israel.

God gave a final, clear warning that no leavened food could be eaten anywhere the people lived. True worship was not meant to stay in public meetings, but had to be lived out at the family dinner table. Obeying this simple rule in the home showed total dedication to the Lord.

Moses gathered the elders of Israel and passed along the Lord's instructions to them. He told each elder to lead their family in choosing and slaughtering the Passover lamb. As leaders, the elders were responsible for making sure the whole community obeyed God's voice.

The elders were instructed to take a bunch of the hyssop plant, dip it into the bowl of blood, and brush it onto the doorposts. Moses also warned that no one was to step outside their home until morning. Staying behind the blood-marked door was their only protection from the coming destruction.

As the Lord moved through Egypt to bring judgment, He would see the blood on the doorframe and shield that doorway from harm. God would not let the destroying angel enter any home marked by the blood. The people were saved not by their own strength, but by trusting in the Lord's promise and the blood of the sacrifice.

Moses commanded the people to keep this festival as a permanent rule for themselves and their children forever. While the sprinkling of blood on doorposts belonged only to that first night in Egypt, the feast of the Passover was to continue through all future generations. It stood as an unending celebration of God's deliverance.

God told the people that they were to continue observing the Passover even after they entered the land of Canaan. Long before they crossed the desert, God spoke with certainty about giving them the land He had promised to Abraham. Practicing the feast in their new home would keep them from forgetting God's past faithfulness.

The unusual customs of the Passover meal were designed to spark the curiosity of children at the table. When the children asked what the ceremony meant, parents had a built-in opportunity to share the story of God's rescue. Passing down the faith to the next generation was built right into the annual celebration.
